raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old South Asian male farmer with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with chest pain and generalized myalgias. He was exposed to "flood waters" a week before admission. He also reported fever and "flu-like" symptoms, which seemingly resolved 2 days before seeking medical care. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and denied using alcohol or any illicit substances. There was no pertinent travel or pet history.
His vital signs on admission were blood pressure of 86/58 mm Hg, heart rate of 102 beats per minute, pulse-oximetry 94% on room air, random blood glucose 184 mg/dL, and temperature of 36.4  C. On physical examination, he was noted to be severely icteric. He had an S3 with no murmurs. Air entry was decreased, and there were occasional scattered crackles bilaterally. His abdomen was mildly distended, however, nontender. He was alert and oriented without any neurological deficits, and there was no anasarca with mild pitting edema to the tibial tuberosity bilaterally. His chest radiography revealed borderline cardiomegaly with mild interstitial edema, and initial admission 12-lead electrocardiogram indicated sinus rhythm at 94 beats per minute with no acute dynamic changes. The patient was immediately resuscitated with intravenous crystalloid infusion, and his electrolytes were repleted judiciously. His coronavirus rapid antigen test returned a negative result.
He was subsequently admitted to the medical intensive care unit, where he was empirically initiated on renally-dosed intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and tigecycline for suspected leptospirosis infection. He also received the routine management bundle for severe sepsis, excluding corticosteroid therapy. The following day, the patient incurred respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia and was commenced on high-flow noninvasive ventilation. A bedside 2-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a moderate global hypokinesis with an estimated ejection fraction of 30% to 35% and mild-moderate mitral regurgitation. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed basilar, bilateral air-space disease suggestive of aspiration pneumonitis. Eventually, his serologies returned positive for leptospirosis infection (Table 1).
The patient endured a rocky clinical course. He alternated rapidly between AT, AF with rapid ventricular response, and VT, for which he was defibrillated and started on low-dose amiodarone infusion at 0.5 mg/min with vigilant hepatic function monitoring (Image 1). During his ensuing hospitalization, he remained clinically unstable and could not undergo further diagnostic testing to clinch or ascertain his tentative diagnosis of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and myocarditis. He deteriorated into a vicious spiral of septic and cardiogenic shock for which he was admitted on multiple inotropic supports; however, he ultimately succumbed to his illness due to multiorgan failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male presenting with chest pain and generalized myalgias following floodwater exposure one week prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week prior to admission, the patient was exposed to floodwaters. He subsequently developed fever and 'flu-like' symptoms, which appeared to resolve 2 days before seeking care. He presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain and generalized myalgias. Following admission, he rapidly deteriorated into severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow noninvasive ventilation, followed by complex cardiac arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and multiorgan failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical history. Farmer by occupation. Lifelong non-smoker, denied alcohol or illicit substance use. No pertinent travel or pet history. Epidemiological exposure: direct exposure to floodwaters one week prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports generalized myalgias, acute chest pain, and prior flu-like symptoms. Denies illicit substance or alcohol use. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals on admission: blood pressure 86/58 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/min, pulse oximetry 94% on room air, random blood glucose 184 mg/dL, temperature 36.4 °C. General: severely icteric, alert and oriented without neurological deficits. Cardiovascular: S3 gallop present, no murmurs heard. Respiratory: decreased air entry bilaterally with occasional scattered crackles. Abdomen: mildly distended, non-tender. Extremities: no anasarca, mild pitting edema extending to bilateral tibial tuberosities.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiography showed borderline cardiomegaly with mild interstitial edema. Initial 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 94 beats/min with no acute dynamic changes; subsequent ECGs revealed rapid alternation between atrial tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and ventricular tachycardia (defibrillated). Bedside 2D transthoracic echocardiogram showed moderate global hypokinesis with an estimated ejection fraction of 30% to 35% and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. Coronavirus rapid antigen test was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed basilar, bilateral air-space disease suggestive of aspiration pneumonitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis infection confirmed by positive serologies, complicated by severe sepsis, acute non-ischemic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis, malignant cardiac arrhythmias (atrial tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, ventricular tachycardia), cardiogenic and septic shock, and acute respiratory failure with aspiration pneumonitis. COVID-19 infection was ruled out.
Plan & Treatment: Emergent intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and judicious electrolyte repletion; empirical renally-dosed IV piperacillin-tazobactam and tigecycline; routine severe sepsis management bundle (corticosteroids withheld); high-flow noninvasive ventilation; electrical defibrillation and low-dose amiodarone infusion at 0.5 mg/min with hepatic monitoring; multiple inotropic supports for refractory shock.
Outcome: Patient developed refractory mixed cardiogenic and septic shock and succumbed to multiorgan failure.
